summary: For ages 9-10: interpret negative whole numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance), place them on a number line, order mixed positive/negative sets, count forwards and backwards through zero, and find simple intervals that cross zero by counting the gap through zero (e.g. −4°C rising 7° reaches 3°C). Keep the work count- and interval-based in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years. Core misconceptions to confront: ordering negatives by magnitude (believing −4 > −1) and miscounting when crossing zero.
misconceptions: Counting the interval across zero wrongly (forgetting the zero step or double-counting it).
Treating a negative as just its digit (ignoring sign).
Applying whole-number intuitions (bigger digit = bigger) to negatives.

activities.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line
steps: Set a starting value in a real context, e.g. the temperature is −4°C, marked on a vertical thermometer or horizontal number line.
Apply a change, e.g. 'it rises by 7 degrees', and move a marker one step at a time, saying each value aloud: −4 → −3 → −2 → −1 → 0, then 1 → 2 → 3.
Deliberately split the count into two parts: how many steps up to reach zero (4), then how many steps beyond zero (3), and record the landing value (3°C).
Count backwards through zero as well: start at 3 and step down in ones — 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 — saying what comes after 0, so you can move both forwards and backwards across zero.

Switch the SAME line into a different context — sea-level depth or a bank balance — keep the start and change equivalent, and notice the number behaves identically even though it means something different.
State in words where you crossed zero and why the total rise is 7 even though you land on 3.
activities.insight: An interval that spans zero is found by counting the gap along the line through zero — so many steps up to zero, then so many more beyond — not by a sign rule; you can count both forwards and backwards across zero, and negatives in different contexts behave the same positionally.

activities.title: Order and place mixed negatives and positives
steps: Arrange a mixed set such as −4, −1, 0, 2, 5 from smallest to largest on a number line.
Place a single value such as −3 at its correct spot on a labelled line.
Decide which of two values is colder/lower/more in debt, e.g. 'Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C?', and justify using position on the line.
Explain why −4 is smaller than −1 even though 4 is a bigger digit than 1, referencing left-is-less on the line.
activities.insight: On the number line, further left (colder / lower / deeper in debt) means smaller, so −4 < −1 < 0 < 2 < 5 — the size of the digit does not decide the order for negatives.

activities.title: Explain the context (optional spoken/role-play extension)
steps: Take on a role such as a submarine pilot describing depths below sea level, or a weather presenter describing temperature changes.

Pose and answer questions like 'We were at −30 m and rose 12 m — where are we now?' (−18 m, still below the surface) and 'It was −3°C and rose 8° — how warm now?' (+5°C, passing up through zero), and explain the crossing of zero where it happens.
Reason aloud about which depth/temperature is higher or lower and how you know.
activities.insight: Negatives describe real quantities (depth, temperature, balance); talking through changes rehearses counting through zero in meaningful situations, while noting that not every change actually crosses zero.

checkQuestion: Ask: 'The temperature is −4°C and it rises by 7 degrees. What is it now, and how did you work it out?'
checkAnswer: 3°C. Count up 7 from −4: four steps reach 0, then three more reach 3 — you pass through zero.
